## TL;DR

This QA pass added automated coverage for the Hub server list refresh gesture and several parallel close-out scheduler boundaries. The existing implementations behaved correctly in the tested cases, so no production code changes were needed. All added and existing focused tests passed after correcting a test import path. These tests exercise Vue component events and the scheduler with controlled promises; they do not replace native-device gesture testing or exercise a real repository lock holder, mobile network, or runner host.

## Work and rationale

I started by reading the task specification, locating the Hub component tests, and inspecting the scheduler and its existing crash and parallel-validation suites. The refresh interaction was already covered for a downward pull at the top and a touch begun on the row menu. Existing cases also verify that the active indicator is rendered. Coverage did not explicitly guard against an upward swipe, a pull while the list is already scrolled, a second refresh event from continued movement after crossing the threshold, or a new gesture while refresh is active. Those cases matter because this component shares touch handling with native list scrolling and row actions.

I added component tests for those gesture boundaries in the existing mobile server-list test. The tests dispatch touch events directly on the mounted list, inspect whether the refresh event was emitted, and set `scrollTop` to model a list away from its top edge. Repeated moves beyond the threshold verify that one gesture triggers exactly one refresh. Mounting with `refreshing: true` verifies that a concurrent pull cannot start another refresh. The existing row-menu case remains in place and still passes.

Timeout and all-unreachable outcomes live below the component in Hub’s health-check validation function. I added focused automated tests using injected fetch implementations, without issuing any network requests. One fetch rejects when the validator’s abort signal fires, verifying the timeout result tells the user the server did not answer. A second case returns HTTP 503 for every server and verifies each result is marked unreachable with an actionable response status. The refresh caller already updates each server’s reachability from those validation results and clears its busy state in a `finally` block; no defect appeared in the behavior inspected here.

For close-outs, the repository already had substantial tests for validation concurrency, publisher ordering, crash retries, bounded give-up, successful crash-count reset, and the parked publisher’s publish-turn behavior. I added a scheduler test for status notifications and a blocked run representing time spent waiting on a lock. It confirms a running lock waiter retains its slot, a pump does not duplicate that task, another run can fail independently, and the scheduler reports state changes through its callback. Releasing the controlled wait models the timeout exit and frees the slot. Existing crash tests were also run to exercise scheduler recovery after a thrown run and the handoff retry path.

No production fix was warranted by the automated cases. I did not create product UI proposals because this pass uncovered no new user-facing design need.

## Approaches tried

I first reused the existing Vue Test Utils setup rather than introducing a separate gesture harness. This keeps the event tests close to the actual component and preserves the same jsdom assumptions as the existing Hub tests. For network outcomes, I used the validator’s injected fetch function so timeout and all-unreachable cases are deterministic and offline. For scheduler lock waiting, I used a manually released promise instead of a real lock file or runner, making it possible to assert the in-flight set at each step without environmental timing or external processes.

The first focused run failed to resolve the new reachability test’s import because its relative path climbed one directory too far from `src/ui-app/tests`. I corrected the path and reran the tests successfully. This was a test setup error, not a product failure.

## Challenges and blockers

A DOM event test cannot model every detail of iOS or Android gesture arbitration, touch cancellation, scroll inertia, haptics, or the Capacitor WebView. The tests cover the component’s explicit logic with synthetic events, but no real phone or simulator was used, as required by this task. The timeout case verifies how an abort is interpreted; it does not measure real network latency or prove that every platform’s fetch implementation delivers abort promptly.

The close-out scheduler test controls the run promise to represent lock waiting and timeout completion. It does not acquire a real repository publication lock, kill/restart the RepoOS process, connect to runner machines, or perform a real parallel publish. Crash retry and parked publication behavior are covered in the existing automated suites, while this pass focuses on state transitions that can be verified locally without real runner hosts.

## Key learnings

The refresh component’s behavior is separated cleanly: it owns gesture eligibility and emits one refresh event, while the application performs reachability checks and owns the busy flag. Testing both layers independently gives deterministic coverage for gesture conflicts and network outcomes without spinning up the Hub. For the scheduler, a controlled unresolved promise is an effective stand-in for a lock wait because it exposes whether capacity remains occupied and whether the pump can accidentally schedule a duplicate. A real native-device QA pass would still be needed to establish how the WebView arbitrates these events during momentum scrolling and actual touch cancellation.
